# Why p-values are useless {#sec-appendix-p-values}













A few years ago I got a reviewer comment that's stuck with me since: "the effect looks promising, but p = 0.052, so this result is not significant — please repeat the experiment with a larger cohort." Same effect size. Same confidence interval, practically. One more decimal place and the entire verdict flips from "no effect" to "publishable." I remember staring at that comment and feeling something between annoyance and vertigo — not because the reviewer was unusually harsh, but because they were doing exactly what they'd been trained to do, what I'd been trained to do, what every methods course I ever sat through treated as simply how science works. Somewhere between Fisher's desk in the 1920s and that reviewer's inbox, a rule of thumb calcified into a verdict. This appendix is about how that happened, and why every model in this book deliberately reports something else instead.

## What a p-value actually measures

Think of a smoke alarm. It's built to answer exactly one narrow question: is there smoke in the air right now, more than the tiny background amount you'd expect on an ordinary day? It doesn't tell you how big the fire is. It doesn't tell you whether to evacuate, call the fire department, or just open a window because someone burned toast. A p-value is that smoke alarm, wired to your data instead of your kitchen. It answers one question — *if the effect I'm testing for were truly, exactly zero, how surprising would data like mine be?* — and nothing else. It doesn't tell you how big your effect is. It doesn't tell you how confident to be in it. It doesn't even tell you whether the effect is real, only how unusual your numbers would look under a hypothesis you almost certainly don't believe anyway (more on that in a moment).

Formally: the p-value is the probability, computed under the assumption that the null hypothesis is exactly true, of observing a result as extreme or more extreme than the one you actually got. That's a statement about the data's surprisingness given an assumption, not a statement about how large your effect is or how much you should trust it — two completely different questions that "p < 0.05" gets asked to answer every day.

## The null hypothesis nobody actually believes

Here's the sharp-point null hypothesis that almost every p-value in the biomedical literature is testing: the true effect is exactly zero, to infinite decimal places, and there is exactly zero systematic error in how you collected and processed the data. Ask yourself honestly: do you believe that's true for, say, cerebral ischemia's effect on GFAP intensity? Not "small" or "hard to detect" — *exactly* zero? Of course not. Biology doesn't produce effects that are exactly nothing; it produces effects that are small, or noisy, or swamped by everything else going on in an animal, but a genuinely exact zero essentially never happens [@mcshane2019]. Which means that with enough animals, enough sections, enough statistical power, you will eventually find "significance" for almost anything — not because you discovered something real, but because you finally had enough data to detect a difference that was never exactly zero to begin with, however biologically trivial. A p-value conflates "detectable" with "important," and those are not the same word.

Let's make that concrete instead of just asserting it, because it's the kind of thing that's easy to nod along to and easy to forget the next time a p-value crosses your desk.

The comparison a reader most needs to see with their own eyes is two "results" that land on opposite sides of the 0.05 line for reasons that have nothing to do with how big or important the underlying effect is. So instead of chasing a canonical example from a textbook, let's build one ourselves — a huge sample chasing a genuinely tiny effect, and a small sample chasing a genuinely large one — and put both through exactly the same significance test.






::: {#tbl-appendix_pvalue_sim .cell tbl-cap='Two simulated studies, nearly identical p-values, wildly different effects'}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(22)

big_n_a <- rnorm(6000, mean = 50, sd = 10)
big_n_b <- rnorm(6000, mean = 50.5, sd = 10)
huge_sample_tiny_effect <- t.test(big_n_b, big_n_a)

small_n_a <- rnorm(8, mean = 50, sd = 10)
small_n_b <- rnorm(8, mean = 60, sd = 10)
tiny_sample_huge_effect <- t.test(small_n_b, small_n_a)

sim_results <- data.frame(
  study = c("Huge sample, trivial effect (n = 6,000/group)",
            "Tiny sample, large effect (n = 8/group)"),
  estimate = c(mean(big_n_b) - mean(big_n_a), mean(small_n_b) - mean(small_n_a)),
  ci_low   = c(huge_sample_tiny_effect$conf.int[1], tiny_sample_huge_effect$conf.int[1]),
  ci_high  = c(huge_sample_tiny_effect$conf.int[2], tiny_sample_huge_effect$conf.int[2]),
  p_value  = c(huge_sample_tiny_effect$p.value, tiny_sample_huge_effect$p.value)
)

library(gt)
gt(sim_results) |> fmt_number(columns = c(estimate, ci_low, ci_high, p_value), decimals = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
\begin{table}
\fontsize{12.0pt}{14.4pt}\selectfont
\begin{tabular*}{\linewidth}{@{\extracolsep{\fill}}lrrrr}
\toprule
study & estimate & ci\_low & ci\_high & p\_value \\ 
\midrule\addlinespace[2.5pt]
Huge sample, trivial effect (n = 6,000/group) & 0.369 & 0.010 & 0.728 & 0.044 \\ 
Tiny sample, large effect (n = 8/group) & 11.786 & -0.842 & 24.414 & 0.065 \\ 
\bottomrule
\end{tabular*}
\end{table}

:::
:::






Both studies land right on the 0.05 boundary — one just under, one just over. Plotted side by side, the actual difference between them is impossible to miss:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(sim_results, aes(x = estimate, y = study, color = study)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), linewidth = 1, size = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Estimated group difference", y = NULL) +
  Plot_theme +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Same significance boundary, opposite scientific story](appendix-p-values_files/figure-pdf/fig-appendix_pvalue_sim-1.pdf){#fig-appendix_pvalue_sim}
:::
:::






The huge-sample study found a difference of half a unit — likely too small to matter biologically in almost any assay — and called it significant, because six thousand animals per group is enough to detect almost anything. The tiny-sample study found a difference twenty times larger, plausibly a real and important biological effect, and called it *not* significant, because eight animals per group barely constrains anything. If you only read the p-values, you'd walk away with exactly the wrong impression of which result deserves your attention. That's not a contrived edge case — it's what a p-value does by construction, because it was never built to measure the thing "significant" makes readers assume it measures.

## Where "p < 0.05" actually came from

It's worth knowing this isn't a law of nature — it's a specific historical accident, and knowing the story makes it much harder to treat 0.05 as sacred.

::: callout-tip
### A threshold born from hand calculation, not statistical theory

Ronald Fisher popularized 0.05 in his 1925 *Statistical Methods for Research Workers* — the book that first put significance testing into the hands of working scientists, rather than mathematicians. He picked it, by his own account, because it's roughly two standard deviations from the mean of a normal distribution, a convenient round number in an era when researchers looked up test statistics in printed tables rather than computing exact p-values by machine [@kennedyshaffer2019]. It was a rule of thumb for a world without computers, not a discovery about how much evidence science requires. Tellingly, Fisher's own tables listed multiple thresholds — 0.05, 0.01, and others — because even he didn't think one number fit every situation. Decades later he wrote plainly that "no scientific worker has a fixed level of significance at which, from year to year, and in all circumstances, he rejects hypotheses" [@kennedyshaffer2019] — a fairly direct disavowal of the very ritual his name now anchors.

There's a second complication most textbooks skip entirely: the 0.05 threshold most of us were taught isn't even Fisher's. Around the same time, Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson built a genuinely different framework, one where you fix an error rate *in advance* as a deliberate decision about acceptable risk, weighed against the consequences of being wrong — not as a post-hoc verdict on a single p-value. Fisher and the Neyman–Pearson camp argued bitterly about this for decades, and neither side would recognize — let alone endorse — the "hybrid" that ended up in most applied statistics textbooks: report a continuous p-value like Fisher, but also declare victory or defeat at a fixed 0.05 like Neyman–Pearson, as though the two frameworks were interchangeable pieces of the same procedure [@kennedyshaffer2019]. The ritual that decided your manuscript's fate was never actually endorsed, whole, by anyone who helped invent its parts.
:::

## The cliff at 0.05, and what falling off it costs you

Treating 0.05 as a cliff edge — significant on one side, nothing on the other — creates a specific, well-documented failure mode: two results that are barely different from each other get treated as categorically different conclusions, while two results that are wildly different can both get filed under the same label. Andrew Gelman and Hal Stern put this about as sharply as it can be put: the difference between "significant" and "not significant" is not itself statistically significant [@wasserstein2019]. Our simulated studies above are exactly that point made concrete — 0.044 and 0.065 aren't meaningfully different numbers, but the ritual insists on treating them as opposite verdicts.

::: callout-tip
### Even the experts get this wrong — so don't feel bad, just get it right going forward

If it's any comfort, misreading a p-value isn't a personal failing — it's close to universal. In one study, psychology professors, lecturers, and students were shown a single t-test result and asked to judge six true-or-false statements about what the p-value meant. Every one of the six statements was false. None of the 45 students caught that. Neither did most of the professors — including the ones who taught statistics for a living [@mcshane2019]. If you've ever quietly nodded along to "p = 0.03 means there's a 3% chance this is a fluke," you're in very well-credentialed company. The fix isn't feeling bad about it; it's building the habit this book keeps returning to — ask what an interval actually says, not what a single threshold seems to imply.
:::

## What we do instead: ask how much, and how sure

None of this means p-values are forbidden or that this book pretends significance testing doesn't exist — you'll see one mentioned occasionally, reported honestly as a continuous number rather than a verdict. But the default habit this book builds, chapter after chapter, is different: report an effect size and an interval, and let the reader judge magnitude and precision for themselves instead of outsourcing that judgment to a single threshold. This approach has a name in the literature — Cumming and Calin-Jageman call it simply asking "how much, how uncertain, and what else is known" [@calinjageman2019]. Their favorite illustration happens to be a neuroscience one: a widely cited study reported that intranasal oxytocin significantly increased trust in humans (p = 0.029), and that single word — significant — turned an intriguing pilot result into a claim cited thousands of times. Reanalyzed as an effect size with a confidence interval, the same data told a much more honest story: an estimated 12.5% increase in trust behavior, with a 90% interval running from a fraction of a percent up to 37.5% [@calinjageman2019]. That interval is not a disappointing downgrade from "significant" — it's simply what the data can actually support, stated plainly instead of laundered through a threshold.

This is exactly the habit you already met in @sec-intro-applied-modeling, dressed up in different data: an effect and an interval, not a verdict. Every `brms`/`parsnip` pair in this book reports one of two kinds of interval for precisely that reason — a confidence interval's long-run coverage guarantee, or a credible interval's direct probability statement about the effect itself, but never a bare "significant" or "not significant" standing in for either. The authors of the ASA's own call to move beyond p < 0.05 summed up the replacement habit in four words worth keeping taped above your desk: *accept uncertainty; be thoughtful, open, and modest* [@wasserstein2019].

That reviewer who flagged my p = 0.052 wasn't wrong to want more certainty — more animals genuinely would have narrowed that interval, and that's a reasonable thing to ask for. What was wrong was the implicit claim that 0.052 and 0.048 represent different scientific conclusions rather than the same modest amount of evidence, described to three decimal places of false precision. Report the effect. Report how sure you are. Let the threshold go.
